# Build vs Buy & Migrations: Trade-off Analysis, Data Consistency, Cutover Planning ## First Principles: The Build vs Buy Decision **Build:** Write software yourself. Full control, can customize, but you own maintenance cost. **Buy:** Use a third-party product (SaaS, vendor, open-source). Lower maintenance, but less control, risk of vendor lock-in. **Migrate:** Switch from one system to another (Build→Buy, Buy→Build, or Build→Build). This is the hard part—moving live data without downtime. ``` Build: Pros: Custom, no vendor risk, cheaper long-term if complex Cons: Engineering cost, maintenance burden, slower to launch Buy (SaaS): Pros: Faster launch, vendor handles operations, less engineering Cons: Less customizable, vendor risk, monthly cost Migrate: Pros: Fix mistakes from bad initial choice Cons: Risk of data loss, downtime, customer impact Cost: 2–3x the implementation cost of original system ``` --- ## The Problem: Legacy System is Choking Your company built an in-house CMS 5 years ago. It works, but: ``` Issues: - Takes 8 weeks to add a field - 40% of engineering time spent on operational tasks (backups, migrations) - New hires can't understand the codebase - Performance is acceptable but expensive (3 database servers) - Can't scale to new product line (SaaS multi-tenant model) Customer impact: - Product team waits for engineering to add features - Outages every quarter (2–4 hours) - Competitors iterate 2x faster Decision: Build anew or buy ContentfulStack? ``` --- ## Build vs Buy Decision Matrix Before you migrate, decide: keep building or switch? ```mermaid graph TD A["Is this core to

New CMS running in shadow mode (writes only, no reads) - Old CMS is source of truth - Validation: diff records from both systems every hour - Risk: dual-write fails mid-transaction Week 3–4: Backfill + reconciliation - Write historical data to new CMS - Validate all 500K records match - Fix discrepancies (schema mapping, type coercion) - Risk: data mismatch not caught until go-live Week 5–6: Read-from-new phase - 10% of users read from new CMS - Monitor error rates, latency - If good: increase to 50%, then 100% - Risk: edge cases only hit at high volume (canary fails) Week 7: Cutover - All traffic on new CMS - Old system still running (fallback) - Risk: bug discovered post-cutover, need to rollback Week 8: Sunset old system - Wait 1 week (no incidents) - Turn off old CMS - Decommission servers - Cost savings: $200K/year ``` **Failure scenario:** ``` Week 5: Deploy canary - 10% traffic to new CMS - P99 latency: 800 ms (expected <400 ms) - Root cause: missing index on popular query Decision point: Option A: Fix index, wait 1 week for stability, retry canary Option B: Continue with 800 ms latency (customers notice) Option C: Rollback to old system, restart plan Best choice: Option A Trade-off: 1 extra week, but safe cutover Alternative: Accept latency risk (not acceptable for live system) ``` --- ## Dual-Write and Reconciliation The most critical step is validation: ``` Dual-write example: Request arrives: POST /content/create?title=... ↓ ├→ Write to old CMS (synchronous) └→ Write to new CMS (async, best-effort) Problem: Async write fails, old has data but new doesn't Solution: Async queue + retry logic Request arrives: POST /content/create ├→ Write to old CMS (synchronous) ├→ Queue async job: "write-to-new-cms" └→ Return 200 OK Background job: ├→ Write to new CMS (retry 3x) ├→ Log reconciliation record └→ Alert if 3 retries fail Validation (hourly): ├→ SELECT COUNT from old CMS → 500,000 records ├→ SELECT COUNT from new CMS → 499,900 records └→ Diff: 100 missing → investigate + backfill ``` --- ## Cutover Patterns: Four Strategies **Pattern 1: Big Bang (risky)** ``` Old system is live Monday 5 PM. Switch all traffic Tuesday 10 AM. Risk: Any bug affects all users immediately. Only use: small systems with simple data model. ``` **Pattern 2: Canary (recommended)** ``` Monday: 90% old, 10% new Tuesday: 70% old, 30% new (if no errors) Wednesday: 50/50 Thursday: 100% new Risk: Gradual, issues caught early. Best for: most systems. ``` **Pattern 3: Feature Flag (safest)** ``` New system deployed but unused. Feature flag "use_new_cms": false Week 1: Gradually enable for 1%, 10%, 50%, 100% of users Risk: Lowest, because feature flag lets you flip instantly. Best for: user-facing changes. ``` **Pattern 4: Parallel Running (most expensive)** ``` Old system and new system both live. Compare results for days/weeks. Cut over only when confident. Risk: Cost is high, but certainty is guaranteed. Best for: critical systems (payment, medical records). ``` --- ## When to Use / When NOT to Use Approaches | Scenario | Build | Buy | Notes | |----------|-------|-----|-------| | Payment processing | NO | YES | Too risky to build; vendor has scale | | CMS for 10M users | NO | YES | Contentful, Sanity proven at scale | | Internal tooling | YES | NO | Quick to build, rarely used, not worth vendor cost | | Recommendation engine | MAYBE | YES | Vendor (e.g., Algolia) is good; build if special needs | | Authentication | NO | YES | Auth0, Okta are battle-tested; don't build | | Real-time analytics | YES | MAYBE | Build for control; buy if latency isn't critical | | Email service | NO | YES | SendGrid, Mailgun proven; complexity is hidden | --- ## Story Card: Failed Migration (Data Corruption) **Setup:** Company is migrating from in-house database to managed PostgreSQL. **Mistake:** Engineer skips dual-write validation step to save time. ``` Wednesday: Deploy new system, canary 10% Thursday: All users switched to new system Thursday 2 PM: Customer reports missing orders Thursday 3 PM: Investigation: 5% of orders from past 6 months are missing Thursday 4 PM: Root cause found - Migration script had a bug (corrupt timestamp parsing) - Affected orders from before June 2024 - 50K orders affected, $2M in revenue records at risk Response: 1. Rollback to old system (2 hours, customers unhappy) 2. Re-run migration with fix (careful validation this time) 3. Canary again, slowly, 1% → 10% → 50% → 100% 4. Cutover: 2 weeks later (not Thursday) Cost of mistake: - 2 weeks of delayed cutover - 2 days of engineering debugging - Customer trust: "Did we lose my data?" (no, but scary) - Could have been prevented by: dual-write + hourly reconciliation Lesson: Skip validation to save 1 week → cost 2 weeks later ``` --- ## Reasoning Framework: Build vs Buy vs Migrate ``` Step 1: Identify the problem - Is the current system actually the bottleneck? - Is it blocking growth or just annoying? - Measure: how much time/cost does it cause? Step 2: Evaluate options Option A: Keep building in-house - Cost: 3 engineers * $200K = $600K/year - Control: 100%, customizable, no vendor risk Option B: Buy SaaS - Cost: $120K/year, setup $20K - Control: 20%, limited customization, vendor risk Option C: Hybrid (buy core, build extensions) - Cost: $120K + 1 engineer = $220K/year - Control: 60%, balanced Step 3: Estimate migration cost - Dual-write phase: 1 month - Validation: 1 month - Canary: 2 weeks - Total: 2–3 months, 1–2 engineers - Risk: data loss or extended downtime Step 4: Decide based on: - Is it core to business? (pay to build) - Is vendor risk acceptable? (buy if yes) - What's the 10-year cost? (use that number) - Can you afford 2–3 month migration? (affects decision) ``` --- ## Q&A (Built on Fundamentals) **Recall 1:** You're evaluating whether to build or buy a CMS. What questions should you ask? *Must-say:* - Is CMS core to our product differentiation? - What are unique requirements we can't buy? - What's the 5–10 year cost of building vs buying? - What's our vendor risk tolerance? **Probe 1:** You decide to buy Contentful. Now you need to migrate your old CMS data. What's your first step? *Expected:* - Write a migration plan (design doc) - Define data mapping (old schema → new schema) - Plan dual-write phase (both systems live) - Plan validation (reconciliation hourly, resolve mismatches) **Probe 2:** Your migration plan says "cutover next Tuesday." Your validation finds 5% data mismatch. What do you do? *Expected:* - Do NOT cutover Tuesday. Too risky. - Investigate mismatches (schema mapping? data corruption?) - Fix root cause - Revalidate until 100% match or acceptable error rate - Then cutover (maybe 1 week later) - This is the right call even if it delays launch. **Numeric 1:** Build a CMS costs 3 engineers * $200K/year. Buy Contentful is $120K/year + $20K setup. When does "buy" break even with "build"? *Working:* - Annual delta: $200K (build) - $120K (buy) = $80K/year - Break-even: $20K (setup) / $80K (annual) = 3 months - After 3 months, buy is cheaper every year - If you keep it 5 years: buy saves $80K * 5 = $400K total **Numeric 2:** Your migration plan has a dual-write phase (1 month) and validation phase (1 month). If dual-write fails 2% of the time and you discover mismatches hourly, how many mismatches do you expect to find before cutover? *Working:* - 2 months = 60 days = 1,440 hours - Hourly validation: 1,440 checks - 2% failure rate: 1,440 * 0.02 = 28.8 mismatches expected - So plan to find ~30 mismatches, fix them, revalidate - This is normal. Accept it. --- ## Questions for the Interviewer - Have you done a major migration? What went wrong? - How do you decide build vs buy in your org? - What's the biggest risk in a live system migration? - How do you validate data consistency across two systems? - Have you had to rollback a migration? What did you learn? --- ## Checklist: Migration Readiness - [ ] **1. Plan is documented:** Design doc exists with timeline, phases, rollback procedure - ❌ Wrong: "We'll migrate next month" (no plan) - ✓ Right: Migration plan (doc) with dual-write dates, validation schedule, cutover date, rollback steps - [ ] **2. Data mapping is tested:** You've validated that old schema → new schema works for 100% of records - ❌ Wrong: Assume mapping will work; find bugs at cutover - ✓ Right: Run migration script on copy of prod data, validate row counts and sample records - [ ] **3. Dual-write is async with retries:** Failed writes don't break old system; they queue for retry - ❌ Wrong: Dual-write is synchronous; if new system is slow, old system becomes slow - ✓ Right: Write to old (sync), queue async job to write to new (retry 3x, alert on failure) - [ ] **4. Validation is automated and hourly:** You find mismatches before cutover, not after - ❌ Wrong: Manual spot-checks - ✓ Right: Hourly reconciliation job that counts/diffs records, alerts on mismatch > 0.1% - [ ] **5. Rollback is tested:** You've practiced reverting to old system before cutover - ❌ Wrong: Rollback plan exists but untested - ✓ Right: You've simulated rollback (turn off feature flag, switch traffic back to old system, verify no data loss)
